title: A Three-Minute Evening Practice for Noticing Change
markdown:
# A Three-Minute Evening Practice for Noticing Change

Many readers ask for a reflection exercise that fits into an ordinary evening without requiring a new journal, a timer, or a particular mindset. The practice below is one concrete option. It comes from the theme of impermanence: the observation that a day is never exactly a repeat of the day before it, even when the surface looks familiar. You can try it tonight. It requires no special equipment.

## What the Practice Is

Call it "One Difference, One Same." Near the end of your day, write one sentence about something today that was not true yesterday, and one sentence about something that remained the same. That is the whole exercise.

This is not a gratitude list. It is not a review of what you accomplished or what went wrong. It is not designed to produce a particular mood. The aim is simply to record two observations before you go to sleep, then stop. You do not need to believe in impermanence to use it. You only need to be willing to notice that today is not a copy of yesterday.

## How to Do It Tonight

1. Pick a stopping point. Choose a moment after dinner or just before bed when you are unlikely to be interrupted by a call or a visitor.
2. Choose a surface. A notebook, a loose sheet of paper, or a notes app on your phone all work. You can do this with pen and paper or with your phone. The medium does not change the instruction.
3. Write today's date at the top.
4. Add two short headings: "Different" and "Same."
5. Under "Different," write one sentence. Name something about today that could not have been true yesterday. It might be a word someone said, a change in the weather, a decision you made, or a sound you noticed.
6. Under "Same," write one sentence. Name something that felt unchanged. It might be the chair you sat in, the route you walked, a thought that returned, or the way you prepared coffee.
7. Read both sentences once. Close the notebook or app. Do not edit, expand, or share it unless you want to.
8. If you miss a night, begin again the next evening. There is no record to keep and no streak to protect.

Expect the writing to take two to three minutes. If it takes longer, you are probably editing in your head. Let the sentences be plain.

## Examples and Variations

Here is one possible entry.

Date: October 22

Different: The barista remembered my order, and I was not expecting that.

Same: I walked past the same construction site, and the fence still blocked the view of the river.

The entry does not explain why the barista's memory mattered or what the fence represents. It only marks what changed and what did not.

A second entry might look like this.

Date: November 3

Different: I noticed a crack in the sidewalk that I had not seen before.

Same: I made the same humming sound while washing dishes.

If you feel stuck, look at smaller details: the temperature of the room, the order in which you dressed, a headline you saw. If nothing seems the same, pick a physical object you touched today and note that it was there yesterday too.

You can also reverse the order. Start with "Same" and finish with "Different." The sequence does not matter, and you can write only one sentence on nights when two feels like too much.

Some nights both sentences will be easy. Other nights one will feel forced. Write it anyway and close the book.

If you prefer to do this in the morning, you can write about yesterday instead of today. The structure stays the same: one difference, one same. The time of day is less important than the pause itself.

You might notice patterns over weeks, or you might not. Neither outcome changes how to do the exercise tonight.

You do not need special paper or a dedicated journal. A receipt, a napkin, or a draft email works. The tool is not the practice.
